    Denotations for functions in which variables are ﬁrst-class denotational citizens — or, “variables are data”

    Murdoch J. Gabbay1, Andrea Marin2, and Samuel Rota Bulò2

    1 School of Computer Science

    Heriot-Watt University EDINBURGH EH14 4AS, Scotland murdoch.gabbay@gmail.com

    2 Dipartimento di Informatica Università Ca’ Foscari di Venezia Via Torino 155, 30172 Venezia Mestre, Italy

    marin,srotabul@dsi.unive.it

    Abstract. We promote a denotational semantics in which variables appear as ﬁrst-class elements of the underlying (sets-based) domain. In this way new functions appear which intensionally examine variables and program on them as a form of data, with full access to the ‘name’ of a variable. At the same time, the extensional treatment of variables as representing an ‘unknown element’ is preserved.

    1 Introduction

    In this paper we promote a new semantics of variables in functional programming languages in which variables appear as concrete object in the underlying denotation, and can be programmed on as names — “the semantics gives access to the intension of a variable”. For example, in our semantics there is a function from numbers to booleans such that “” is false, because ‘’ is not equal to ‘’ (intensional equality); there is also a function such that ‘’ may be true or false, depending on what and are (extensional equality). The motivations for this work come from computer science and are discussed below.

    Consider the typed -calculus and its semantics [5], which we now brieﬂy construct: Choose a two-element set and deﬁne types by where indicates the function-set. (It would be more usual to deﬁne a syntax for types and then map types to sets; for our purposes we can take types to be sets.) Fix some countably inﬁnite set of variable symbols or atoms; we use these throughout the paper. Terms are inductively deﬁned by :: quotiented by -equivalence. A typing environment maps atoms to types and a typing judgement is a triple : . The valid typing judgements are inductively deﬁned by:

    We can give terms a semantics as follows: if is a type environment let a valuation be a map from to () (). So maps atoms to elements of their types. Then extends to all terms by:

    Here is the map such that ()( and ()(().

    So far, so standard. As far as we know the idea of valuations is due to Tarski [42]. ML and Haskell [35, 43] are based on the typed -calculus with this semantics (Haskell more than ML since ML has global state, but never mind). They do all right; why should we be wanting any different?

    As always, what we are happy to have depends on what we want to achieve. The semantics above is a useful abstraction for giving denotation to functional programming — but situations do exist which certainly look like functional programming, but where the semantics above is not the perfect abstraction:

    – Suppose that we want patterns as ﬁrst-class entities [3, 27, 11] so that we can pass them as explicit arguments to pattern-matching functions.
    Variables occur in patterns and the usual notion of variable must be modiﬁed in some way because the valuation identiﬁes a variable with its denotation (). We expressly do not want this behaviour when we pass a pattern as an argument, because the variables in a pattern may be later matched to different things in different pattern-matchings.

    – Suppose that we want to pass ‘an explicit substitution’ as a ﬁrst-class entity ([2]) [20, 30, 40] such that (([2])) equals 2. The valuation identiﬁes with () and with (). On the face of it () cannot ‘mention ’ or ‘mention ’, because and live in the meta-level (the syntax; the intension) and () and () live in the denotation (the semantics; the extension).

    – Suppose that we want to examine an intensional property of a term at runtime, such as its free variables fv(). This is not possible because the valuation identiﬁes with (). Yet applications arise where this can be useful, for example if we wish to mix functional and logic programming by adding narrowing to -reduction as a computational step [24] or in logic or programming frameworks where the predicate ‘is a variable’ is made explicit [21, 10].

    – Now consider itself. There is no function in the usual semantics to denote a function --which ‘takes a variable name and an argument and returns ’.
    More generally, it is not possible to give denotations to functions that bind variable names in their arguments, because variables (or to be quite precise, variable names) do not appear in the denotation. One example of such a function which we can imagine, but cannot easily give a denotation to, is -- above; another is any ‘context’ such as -; the famous ‘term with a hole’ used for example in notions of program equivalence [37].

    The references above are just some of many practical instances where the notion of variable name is made explicit in the language. These instances have not assembled themselves under a single denotational banner in anything like the way that functional programing languages are grouped around the banner of the ‘standard’ semantics described above (and its elaborations for practical systems, e.g. to account for global state in ML).

    So this paper will attempt to create a ‘sets and functions between them’ semantics which exhibits by concrete construction certain ideas about how variables can be treated in denotation.

    In discussions this material with colleagues we have noted a list of Frequently Asked Questions. We address them in the text with “ Question Answer” at strategic points.

    How do we know that this is the ‘right’ substitution action? We do not: Deﬁnition 5.2 appears to be what is necessary to make Theorem 5.4 work; there may be other deﬁnitions and we do not yet have an overview of the design space.

    How dare we inﬂict a non-canonical deﬁnition upon the reader? No single modal or temporal logic is canonical; there is a family whose members are useful in linguistics, hardware veriﬁcation, and much more besides. No single notion of truth is canonical either; truth may be classical, intuitionistic, relevant, and so on. The -calculus is non-canonical but useful, and so are the different implementations of ordered pairs in set theory. So our substitution action is non-canonical; it lets us express what we want to express, so what?

    Perhaps we should be really cunning and design an alternative deﬁnition of substitution which is conﬂuent also on function-spaces. No, we should not! Recall that our motivation is to permit programming on variables as names, i.e. as a form of data (a very special form of data, with a substitution action). Conﬂuence effectively guarantees that we can do nothing with a variable that we cannot do with an instantiation of it, or put another way, a conﬂuent substitution set cannot ‘see’ the names of variables in it. Lemma 5.5 makes this point formally, by proving that even if and cannot see their own variables in this sense, the functions between them certainly may. To wish to guarantee conﬂuence is to be blind to the motivation of this paper.

    So where is the programming language to go with this semantics? There is no one programming language to go with a semantics of this style, and even if there were we would have no space to develop it here. The closest we can reasonably get here and now is the discussion in the next section.

Unique least supporting sets are a signiﬁcant practical convenience, at least in our experience.

    7 Conclusions and related work

    A variable has two properties; a name, and the ability to represent an unknown element. Typi-cally, the name of a variable is visible in the syntax of a programming language, but not in its semantics. The transition between these two aspects of the notion of ‘variable’ is traditionally managed by valuations [42].

    The denotation in this paper admits a direct representation of variables in the denotation as names-with-a-substitution-action. This makes valuations ‘go away’, but more importantly it allows us to give denotations to functions which reﬂect on the names of variables; we have in mind functions like substitution, -abstraction, and case-splits on intensional equality of variables (their names), occurrences of variables in elements, functions which bind variables in their arguments, and so on.

    Our immediate future work is to test our semantics on Curry [24] and on a recent language with pattern-matching [3].

    In 1999 the ﬁrst author presented FM sets [23] in work with Pitts. This provided a semantics for -conversion which in time gave rise to useful logics [8] and programming languages [41, 9]. We hope that the semantics of this paper will inspire further logics and programming languages, this time with built-in principles for explicit manipulation of their own variables.

    More questions are: can easily be made into a semantics of classical propositional logic with quantiﬁers, can it be patched for the intuitionistic case [36]? Can we investigate semantics of the untyped -calculus by considering reﬂexive substitution-function-sets [32]? As mentioned at the end of the previous section, we should generalise substitution from to for various , in the style perhaps of [17] and thus obtain novel semantics of systems like predicate logic [25].

    The issue of ‘extension’ versus ‘intension’ is well-known in philosophy and logic [2], and also well-studied in computer-science [26]. The typical example of such a development is ‘how do we distinguish between two different proofs of the same proposition’, or ‘how do we distinguish between two algorithms that compute the same function’; variables are treated as extensionally as always. So far as we know the only intensional study of variables in logic, is -logic [21].

    So far as we know, the only treatments of substitution in a context liable to give semantics to functional programming come from category theory [18, 17]. As we have discussed above, these still treat variables extensionally and are not suitable to program on the name of a variable.

    Treatments exist of substitution in the absence of functions. Crabbé gives axioms [13, 12] in ﬁrst-order logic enriched with (in our terminology) atoms and freshness conditions. The similarities between the two axiomatisations is striking though there are also signiﬁcant differ-ences: for us atoms and freshness conditions are part of an ambient ‘nominal framework’ whose ideas (equivariance, abstractions, support, permutation action on functions) we have fully ex-ploited to deﬁne the substitution action on functions, which Crabbé does not do. Crabbé does not consider functions (‘...we are not concerned with the notion of bound variable’ [12, page 2]’) whereas they are the focus of our enquiry here. Crabbé also adheres to conﬂuence (rule (sub), Crabbé’s axiom 4) as ‘the fundamental axiom of substitution’ [12, page 3] whereas we have repeatedly argued in this paper that for our purposes, this is the axiom to drop!

    Feldman [14] gives an algebraic axiomatisation (our axioms are nominal algebraic [22]). He is inspired by a concrete model of substitution similar to the environment model in Section 4 (we got the construction independently from conversations with Gilles Dowek). Feldman’s axioms are distant from ours being closer in spirit to Cylindric Algebras [7] and Lambda Abstraction Algebras [31, 39].

    Mariño [34] gives a semantics for Curry based on our premise in this paper that variables should exist in denotation. The constructions seem to be concrete instances of the constructions in this paper, without the accompanying theory — but this remains to be checked.

    Combinatory Algebra [5], Illative Combinatory Logic [4] (based on combinatory algebra), and Predicate Functor Logic [29], attain the effect of substitution by emulations. For example see the translation of -terms into combinatory algebra terms [5]. Thanks to the use of combi-nators, variables just ‘go away’.

    We must not forget -calculi with explicit substitutions [1]. Lescanne’s survey [30] and the thesis of Bloo [6] chart a vast literature on the topic. These decompose -reduction as a rule to introduce explicit substitution ( ()[] ), and explicit rules for that substitution’s subsequent behaviour (which is to substitute, of course). These calculi are designed to measure the cost of a -reduction and do not directly reﬂect on variables’ names; for example it is not possible to represent a function which case-splits on whether a variable is bound or not in its argument, or to represent the abstraction - directly, as we do.

    This work beneﬁts greatly from research into nominal techniques. The axiomatisation of substitution we use is inherited from work on nominal algebra [22]. This is descended from but not to be confused with previous less powerful axiomatisations in nominal rewriting [16, 15], itself based on nominal terms and uniﬁcation [44]. Nominal sets go back to [23].

    The NEW calculus of contexts (NEWcc) [20] is a -calculus with constructs which can be partially interpreted in the substitution-sets-and-functions of this paper. The NEWcc has a richer structure including a hierarchy of atoms, and is also weaker structure in that thus far we have not considered case-splits in the NEWcc on equality of names, nor explicit representation of freshness. Transfer of ideas is possible in both directions.

    We see some connection with pointers, which we have yet to make formal. A pointer has some of the properties of a variable in that it represents an unknown element by pointing to it. A pointer also has a name (itself). Pointers are incredibly useful, but also they are notoriously hard to work with. We would like to investigate to what degree our atoms are a semantics for ‘well-behaved pointers’ — note that this is entirely orthogonal to monadic semantics for state, which introduces controlled doses of sequentiality [33] into pure functional programming but which is not speciﬁc to state.

    The semantics of most languages with variables use valuations. This is a formal way of say-ing ‘a variable is an unknown denotational element and nothing but an unknown denotational element’. So subliminally is this notion introduced that we may forget to imagine alternatives. We say: awake! Variables can be so much more!
